title: AI in academia: An overview of selected tools and their areas of application
extended_summary:
This paper addresses the rapidly expanding use of artificial intelligence tools in academic work, especially after the rise of ChatGPT, and asks how educators and researchers can make sense of the available tools, their functions, and their risks. Rather than evaluating one intervention empirically, the paper offers a narrative overview of selected AI applications used in higher education for literature search, paper analysis, and academic writing/editing.

The author approaches the topic from the perspective of a university educator and compiles a review of tools such as Elicit, Litmaps, Scite, ChatPDF, Scholarcy, Jenni.ai, Quillbot, Trinka, and others. The paper describes how these tools support semantic search, citation mapping, document questioning, summarization, paraphrasing, and language correction. It also notes some implementation features, such as use of GPT-4 in certain tools, custom-document-based AI, and integration with citation managers, but does not study classroom deployment or coaching workflows.

The context is higher education rather than K–12, and the paper is centered on academic users: educators, researchers, and students. Its main conclusion is that AI tools can save time, improve readability and writing quality, and support literature work, but they also raise concerns about authenticity, privacy, bias, and academic integrity. The paper emphasizes that users need critical judgment, ethical awareness, and institutional guidance when adopting these tools, because they are best used to complement human work rather than replace it.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generic generative AI / large language model chatbot or writing assistant used for academic tasks such as answering questions, summarizing, drafting, editing, and providing feedback.
identified_tools.use_case: This paper is a narrative review of selected AI tools in academia. It discusses generative AI and LLMs in general, including ChatGPT, GPT-4, and GPT-3, but does not evaluate a specific AI tool in K–12 teacher instructional coaching or lesson-plan feedback.

quality_tier_rationale: This is a narrative review/overview article with no empirical evaluation of an AI tool in K–12 teacher coaching or lesson-plan feedback. The paper summarizes tools and their potential uses rather than testing outcomes.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper argues that AI tools may improve efficiency and quality of academic work, but it reports no measurable effect sizes or outcome data for the target use case. Any impact claims are descriptive and not directly evidenced in this study.
